## The curve of the claim {#the-curve-of-the-claim}

```{r}
#| label: spec-curve
#| fig-width: 9.5
#| fig-height: 4.1
# The curve of 64 (data/spec_curve.csv), the chart that the Multiverse page
# draws, with the reference specification tagged in ink. Built on
# curve_base(), so that the next slide reuses this exact panel.
curve_base() +
  mark_layer(transmute(curve_ref, tag = "the raw gap of the paper", b_pp, rank, sig))
```

::: {.fs-75}
Every combination of the five decisions that keep more than one option: **`r sum(curve$b_pp < 0)` of `r nrow(curve)`** below zero and **`r sum(curve$b_pp < 0 & curve$sig)`** significant at 5%, from **`r fmt_num(min(curve$b_pp), 1)`** to **`r fmt_num(max(curve$b_pp), 1)`** points; randomisation p at most `r fmt_num(max(curve$p_ri), 4)`.
:::

::: {.src}
cases/housing/data/spec_curve.csv: the height of a mark is the estimate in percentage points, its shape the test of its own model (HC2 *t* for the linear model, *z* for the logit).
:::

::: notes
This is the curve of the claim, the same curve over which the Multiverse page draws your results. Sixty-four specifications, every combination of the five decisions that keep more than one option, each one a mark, ranked from the largest gap on the left to the smallest on the right. Every one is a justifiable answer to the claim on these data. Below zero is the direction of the claim, and look: every single mark is below zero, and every one is a circle, which means significant at five per cent under the test of its own model. The randomisation test agrees on every specification. So on these data, direction and significance are not in dispute at all. What moves is the size, from twenty points down to twelve, and there is a visible step in the middle. The tagged mark on the far left is the reference, the raw gap of the paper.
:::

## The published results on the curve {#where-your-result-lands}

```{r}
#| label: spec-overlay
#| fig-width: 9.5
#| fig-height: 4.1
# The same panel with the published result and the five reanalyses
# (data/reference_marks.csv), each placed by its gap in points; the
# published result is tagged "OAs 2017". Marks at the same height share a tag.
curve_base() + mark_layer(marks)
```

::: {.resultline}
Your own results are on the class chart of the [Multiverse](../cases/housing/multiverse.html) page, drawn over this same curve
:::

::: {.src}
cases/housing/data/reference_marks.csv: the published change in predicted probability for the OAs, the course refit of each script for the analysts.
:::

::: notes
The same chart, nothing moved, with six results dropped onto it: the published result of the OAs, tagged OAs 2017, and the five Multi100 analysts. The published result, UYV3F and P9W8Y all sit at the far left, at the raw gap of twenty points, because all three compare Hispanic with white names among the replies, and without covariates a logit reproduces the raw gap exactly. EWFMI adds covariates and sits a little to the right. 8PTRZ, whose number you reproduced, compares with all other names and sits in the middle of the left-hand cluster. And 25N5D, alone, sits in the right-hand cluster, because it counts every delivered email. All six gaps fall within the range of the curve, or at its edge, including the two analyses whose choices lie outside the menu, EWFMI and the published model, so the spread among the analysts is no wider than the spread among the justifiable specifications. Your own results are on the Multiverse page.
:::
